Suppose the first draw is green. The excess of green over red must remain positive after draws one through five and return to zero at draw six. After deleting the first green and final red, the remaining four steps must form a Dyck path: they have equal colour counts and never go below zero relative to the new starting level. There are C2​=2 such orders, GGRR and GRGR, giving GGGRRR and GGRGRR in the original game.
Interchanging green and red gives RRRGGG and RRGRGG. Thus there are
4​

P(X2​≤x∣X1​=x)=⎩⎨⎧​g+r2x​,g+rg+x​,​1≤x≤g,g<x≤r.​​

ii OurBigBook.com
The characteristic equation of the reduced homogeneous linear differential equation is m2−β=0. Its polynomial roots change type with the sign of β, giving
y(t)=⎩⎨⎧​C1​eβ​t+C2​e−β​t,C1​+C2​t,C1​cos(−β​t)+C2​sin(−β​t),​β>0,β=0,β<0.​​
(50)
For β=0, the zero polynomial root is repeated, so the second independent solution is t. For β<0, the polynomial roots are the complex conjugate pair ±i−β​, and the displayed sine and cosine give a real basis of solutions. The constants are arbitrary real numbers. In every case x(t)=y′(t)−cost reconstructs the corresponding general solution of the coupled system.

Write Ψ(η,ξ)=ψ(x,t). The inverse coordinate formulas x=(η+ξ)/2 and t=(η−ξ)/(2c) are valid because c>0. The multivariable chain rule gives
∂x​=∂η​+∂ξ​,∂t​=c∂η​−c∂ξ​.
(110)
Applying these operators twice and using the symmetry of second derivatives,
ψxx​=Ψηη​+2Ψηξ​+Ψξξ​,c21​ψtt​=Ψηη​−2Ψηξ​+Ψξξ​.
(111)
Thus the wave equation is equivalent to
Ψηξ​=0​.
(112)
For each fixed η, the partial derivative Ψη​ has zero derivative with respect to ξ, so it is a function of η alone. Taking an antiderivative in η gives Ψ=f(η)+g(ξ), where the integration constant may depend on ξ. Hence
ψ(x,t)=f(x+ct)+g(x−ct)​.
(113)
Conversely, direct partial differentiation verifies the wave equation for every twice differentiable pair f,g. The two terms describe profiles moving left and right respectively at wave speed c along the characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation.

f′=21​u′+2c1​v,g′=21​u′−2c1​v.
(115)
Fix a reference point x∗​ and set V(x)=∫x∗​x​v(s)ds. Taking antiderivatives gives
f(x)=21​u(x)+2c1​V(x)+K,g(x)=21​u(x)−2c1​V(x)−K​.

The constants must be opposite to preserve the first initial condition; the arbitrary constant of integration K does not change ψ. Substitution yields D'Alembert's formula:
ψ(x,t)=2u(x+ct)+u(x−ct)​+2c1​∫x−ctx+ct​v(s)ds​.

The fundamental theorem of calculus verifies that its time derivative at zero is v(x), and its value at zero is u(x). The oriented integral also makes the formula valid for negative t.

An antiderivative of the initial velocity is −2ce−s2/2. Thus D'Alembert's formula gives
ψ(x,t)=2c1​[−2ce−s2/2]x−ctx+ct​=e−(x−ct)2/2−e−(x+ct)2/2​.
(118)
This is a positive Gaussian function moving right and a negative Gaussian function moving left. Their cancellation at t=0 gives the zero initial displacement, while direct differentiation gives ψt​(x,0)=2cxe−x2/2.
For every t>0, the profile is an odd function of x, vanishes at x=0, is positive for x>0 and negative for x<0, and tends to zero at both spatial infinities. The signs follow from (x+ct)2−(x−ct)2=4xct. The positive and negative lobes move farther apart as t increases; for large separation they approach the individual unit-height Gaussian functions centred at x=±ct. At finite separation the actual extrema lie slightly beyond these centres: writing a=ct, the positive global maximum occurs at the unique x>a satisfying (x−a)/(x+a)=e−2ax.
